sections.html:
• Common name: Dwarf baby tears
  • Other names: Cuba, HC, Pearl Grass
  • Scientific name: Hemianthus callitriodes
  • Lighting: medium to high
  • Substrate: needed
  • Growth rate: slow
  • Placement in tank: foreground (carpeting)
  • Height: 3–5 cm
  • Fertilisers: appreciated
  • CO2: needed
  • Propagation: cuttings, spreads by runners

Dwarf baby tears was first described and collected by Holger Windelov and Eusebio Delgado Perez in 2003 during an expedition to a small rocky stream in Las Pozas, Cuba, about 90 kilometres east of Havana. The plant got the name "Cuba" from its place of origin; it is also called "HC", short for its scientific name Hemianthus callitriodes.

In 2008 aquatic plant farms added it to their cultivation and started selling it in the US. It continues to grow in popularity because of its excellent carpeting ability and is widely available.

It belongs to the family Scrophulariaceae, later changed to Linderniaceae. Classification: Kingdom Plantae; Clade Tracheophytes; Clade Angiosperms; Order Lamiales; Family Scrophulariaceae (Linderniaceae); Genus Hemianthus; Species Hemianthus callitriodes.

Dwarf baby tears or HC dwells in rivers and rocky streams in Cuba, Jamaica and Puerto Rico. It is also adapted for life in nano and medium tanks.

It is a popular and versatile foreground (midground) plant and one of the smallest aquarium plants in the world. It is vibrant bright green overall, except the roots, which are white or cream. It grows up to 3 cm vertically and spreads up to 10 cm horizontally.

The leaves are about a millimetre, roundish-ovoid and fine-textured. Long, thread-like creeping stems (runners) form dense mats or carpets, while tiny roots stay in the substrate, anchoring the plant and absorbing nutrients.

A distinct feature is the production of small pearls of oxygen that stay on top of the plant, adding a lively look to the carpet. If grown emersed, the plant produces tiny white flowers that are easy to overlook.
A minimum tank size of 40 litres is recommended for this plant. It can also do well in nano tanks of 20 litres or medium-sized tanks, depending on your choice and purpose.

Planting and propagation

Split a potted bunch into several sizeable portions. Detach the plant from the rockwool and separate the wool from the roots slowly to avoid tearing them. Divide the plant into small plugs. Each plug should have white roots attached, otherwise it will melt away. Rinse thoroughly and plant in the substrate with tweezers.

The roots are very small and shallow, so the plant is hard to anchor. Insert it deep enough to stop it popping out, while keeping the top well above the substrate. If planted in small clumps a few centimetres apart, it spreads and covers the substrate with individual stems that form bright, dense carpets. It is relatively slow-growing and can take several weeks to cover the area. It can also be attached to driftwood, where it forms large green cushions with overhanging shoots.

It propagates by stem cuttings: take mature plant from the tank, split it into many pieces and replant them.

Dry start method

A popular method is the dry start (growing emersed first, then flooding), which allows growing the plant before cycling the tank and also shows the plant is a great choice for paludariums. After planting, add only enough water to reach the surface of the lowest part of the substrate; do not pour it in directly, as it can damage the substrate, but spread the flow, for example with a garden mister. Plant with tweezers, cover the top of the tank with cling wrap to increase humidity, but not completely, as the plant needs CO2: leave a slit for exchange with ambient air. After about 5 to 8 weeks the tank can be flooded.

  • Pros: easy planting (in water it tends to float up); light (without water, even low light can be enough); natural CO2.
  • Cons: it takes a lot of time before flooding; misting is needed at least once a day; die-offs after adding water, as the leaves are not ready for submerged conditions and many melt away.

Care

The plant is not easy to maintain and needs adequate care. Alternatives are Monte Carlo (small, beautiful and easy to care for), flame moss and Cryptocoryne parva.

  • Gently brush or stir the dense carpet with tweezers to stop it twisting together; this also brings food particles, decayed organic matter and debris to the surface.
  • Dose iron to prevent yellow shoots. Pressurised CO2 and fertiliser are required for proper growth, since it is a slow grower.
  • In nature it lives in clean water, so pay attention to water quality; it does not like foul water.
  • Watch for unhealthy plants and remove them gently. Introduce algae-eating species to remove algae growing on the plants.

Trimming

The plant takes about 4 weeks to form a compact, dense carpet. Trim it frequently with pruning scissors to keep it healthy and dense. If it grows freely, the base of the carpet discolours because light does not reach it, and if the bottom dies the plant dies. When the carpet is thicker than 4–5 cm, the lower parts rot and the whole carpet floats to the surface. Trim the top down to a few centimetres above the ground. If you see white roots with every cut, you have cut too deep: go slow and snip only a thin layer off the top.

After trimming, collect the floating pieces with a fine net. Turn off the filter outflow and any powerheads to make catching them easier.

Problems

  • Melting: leaves tend to melt (turn brown), mainly because of the transfer from emersed to submersed form. Leaves die off until the plant has adapted, then regrow. This takes time.
  • Yellow or white colouring: yellow shoots or stem bases are likely a sign of iron deficiency (such as iron and potassium) or light not reaching the base. Dose iron in adequate quantities.
  • Attachment: the tiny roots often struggle to stay in the substrate, so aqua soil is recommended as a layer over the main substrate to improve anchorage. Wedge the roots back in when the plant pops out.
  • Algae: algae can overrun and kill the plant. It is a slow grower that needs a lot of light, and higher light, CO2 and fertilisers make algae harder to manage.

Temperature: keep the tank at 20–24 °C. The plant is very sensitive to temperature, and there are many recorded cases of it dying off above 25 °C. Check the water temperature regularly with a good digital thermometer.

pH: the optimal pH is 6.0–7.5.

Hardness: the plant appreciates 1–10 dGH and does not like very hard water.

Lighting: the plant is photophilic and cannot grow in dark conditions, so it needs medium to high light for healthy growth. It grows more compact under high light. Lighting duration should be about 10–12 hours daily. About 40–50 PAR of LED light keeps it healthy, but the depth of water (height of the tank) is the real measurement to consider, so small, low tanks may not need powerful lights.

Substrate: it grows best in fine-grained substrates. Nutrient-rich soils such as ADA Amazonia aqua soil or Aqua Soil Powder are ideal because the small grains let the roots grow faster and more easily. Aqua soil also gives a more pleasing look in the foreground thanks to its fine granules. The plant has a weak root system and roots poorly, so choose light, porous substrates in which it roots well.

CO2 and fertilisers: the plant needs steady CO2 injection (10–30 mg/l). It is close to impossible to grow lush, dense carpets for long without CO2 and fertiliser supplementation. If the stems do not creep but point upwards, or the leaves become gradually smaller, it can be a CO2 deficiency. Fertilisers such as Flourish Excel are well accepted. An iron supplement is also essential because the plant is susceptible to iron deficiency, which often leads to yellow shoots.

If you keep shrimp in the tank, note that a high level of CO2 and copper (most fertilisers contain copper) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Benefits

  • Oxygenation: it helps oxygenate the tank water, and its pearling adds oxygen.
  • Aesthetics: a lush green carpet with small, fine-textured foliage in the foreground.
  • Forage ground: dense carpets serve as a forage ground for shrimp, which pick up tiny food particles and organic matter, improving shrimplet survival.
  • Hiding place: the carpets shelter fry and small fish.
  • Breeding: fish can mate and spawn in it.
  • Filtration: it helps keep water stable by absorbing nitrates, which are toxic to fish and shrimp in large amounts.

Tankmates

Be careful with floating plants that can shade it (for example hornwort, Java fern, water wisteria, duckweed, dwarf water lettuce, frogbit).

It is a friendly carpeting species and can be kept with:

  • Dwarf shrimp (all Neocaridina varieties such as Red Cherry, Blue Velvet, Black Rose, Snowball, Orange Sakura, Green Jade and Rili; Caridina species such as Crystal Red, Caridina cf. babaulti and Blue Tiger), Amano shrimp and ghost shrimp. With water flow, also bamboo shrimp and vampire shrimp.
  • Snails (ramshorn, nerite, Malaysian trumpet, Japanese trapdoor, mystery snails, etc.). These pick up tiny food bits and algae from the carpet.
  • Fish such as neon tetras, bettas, swordtails, corydoras, guppies and platies, which are not aggressive towards the plant and often hover around the carpet.

Hostile species such as dwarf gouramis, angelfish, rainbowfish, oscars and herbivorous cichlids should be avoided at all costs because they will tear up the carpets.

Quarantine

Quarantine the plant before putting it in the aquarium. It can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or even predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs, etc.). It could also have been treated with chemicals (pesticides) to remove parasites, snails and so on, and these chemicals are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

Conclusion

Dwarf baby tears is versatile but very capricious, so it is not among the best freshwater plants for beginners and can be hard even for experienced planted-tank keepers. It needs a lot of light, a large amount of CO2 injection, a fine-grained substrate and fertiliser to establish dense, bright green carpets in the foreground.
